content_bullets: Highlight the debate regarding whether looped neural networks and frontier LLMs exhibit genuine reasoning on combinatorial benchmarks like Sudoku-Extreme.

Formulate the comparative evaluation across three distinct solver paradigms: direct LLM adaptive thinking, LLM code synthesis of standard-library Python solvers, and an independent CPU re-implementation of CRAM (Classical Relational Associative Memory).

Summarize direct LLM results: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 solve 30%-60% of test puzzles directly, suffering from token exhaustion at 32,000 tokens and costing up to $0.71 per solved puzzle with median latencies exceeding 100 seconds.

Summarize code synthesis results: single-prompt Python solvers from all three models achieve 100% accuracy (4,500/4,500 solves across 9 solvers and 500 puzzles) in ~1 ms per puzzle at a generation cost of less than $0.06.

Summarize CRAM results: learned CRAM fits in 2.5 s on a consumer CPU and solves 496-497/500 puzzles with zero incorrect stops, perfectly recovering the underlying constraint graph; a hand-set single-weight energy achieves identical accuracy (497/500).

Conclude that for deterministic combinatorial reasoning, programmatic code synthesis is overwhelmingly superior in speed and cost, while Sudoku-Extreme primarily benchmarks constraint satisfaction rather than deep reasoning.
Introduce the recent focus on combinatorial puzzle benchmarks (e.g., Sudoku-Extreme) as tests of looped and recurrent neural reasoning.

Introduce Hoover et al. (arXiv 2611.17309, 2026), who propose CRAM—a learned variant of the Hopfield-Tank energy model—demonstrating 99.996% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme after 42 ms of H200 GPU training.
Frame the competing paradigm: frontier LLMs deployed with extended 'adaptive thinking' to solve puzzles purely in context.
State the lack of controlled, single-budget comparisons evaluating cost, wall-clock latency, and failure modes across these distinct approaches.
Replication and evaluation of CRAM on commodity hardware: independent implementation in NumPy (pseudolikelihood training) and C (focused Gibbs search) running solely on a laptop CPU.
Three-way paradigm comparison: direct LLM reasoning vs. LLM code generation vs. energy-based constraint satisfaction across 500 Sudoku-Extreme instances.

Empirical findings on failure modes: direct LLM reasoning is brittle (token limits and subtle hallucinations), code synthesis is robust (4,500/4,500 successful runs), and learned energy equals hand-set Hopfield-Tank energy.
Explicit confirmation of the original authors' caveat: Sudoku-Extreme is insufficient to demonstrate deep emergent reasoning.
Survey recurrent neural models and looped transformers designed to simulate iterative algorithmic execution.
Discuss the adoption of Sudoku, mazes, and graph algorithms as synthetic tests for neural reasoning capabilities.
Highlight the tension between learning heuristic search patterns and exact constraint propagation.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.3 Classical Energy-Based Models and Associative Memory
content_bullets: Review Hopfield networks and continuous Hopfield-Tank optimization formulations for NP-complete constraint problems.
Examine modern pseudolikelihood estimation techniques for discrete pairwise Markov random fields.
Discuss the CRAM framework (Hoover et al., 2026) and focused Gibbs search mechanisms for finding zero-energy ground states.
Formalize the belief state grid of shape 81 x 9 for opaque cell indices without coordinate priors (no row/column/box knowledge).
Specify the energy function: negative entropy term, pairwise 9x9 coupling matrices between cell pairs, and local bias vectors.
Detail the pseudolikelihood optimization objective implemented in NumPy over 1,000 solved training boards.
Describe the focused Gibbs search inference implemented in C: four parallel random restarts, single CPU core, move budget of 10 million steps.
Formulate the hand-set Hopfield-Tank baseline: zero training parameters, static uniform penalty weight across true constraint peers.
Define the constraint graph peer structure: 20 unique neighbors per cell (8 row peers, 8 column peers, 4 non-overlapping box peers).
Establish the ablation purpose: determining whether learned coupling parameters encode anything beyond simple peer exclusion.

subsections.subsection_title: 3.3 LLM Solver Paradigms: Direct CoT vs. Code Generation
content_bullets: Define the direct CoT protocol using Claude models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5) with adaptive thinking set to high effort and a 32,000-token ceiling.
Define the program synthesis protocol: a zero-shot prompt requesting a standard-library Python Sudoku solver.
Detail the execution sandbox: running synthesized scripts directly on test puzzles via the local Python interpreter.
Describe the hardware platform: a single commodity Apple M4 Pro laptop CPU without GPU acceleration; total API spend constrained to $3.75.
Detail the test dataset: 500 puzzles sampled from sapientinc/sudoku-extreme across 5 random pages (median 26 clues per puzzle).
Explain sample subsets for direct LLM solving (5 puzzles for Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, 10 for Haiku 5.5) dictated by API cost constraints.
Present performance metrics: Opus 5.5 (3/5 solved, median 124.9 s, $0.426/puzzle), Sonnet 5.5 (3/5 solved, median 166.1 s, $0.250/puzzle), Haiku 5.5 (3/10 solved, median 105.7 s, $0.014/puzzle).
Analyze token exhaustion failures: Opus and Sonnet failed on identical puzzles (difficulty 88 and 15) by hitting the 32k-token ceiling.
Analyze incorrect answer generation: Haiku's 2 wrong completions produced boards with 74/81 and 78/81 valid cells while asserting correctness.
Evaluate 9 independently synthesized Python solvers (3 per model): 100% success rate across all 500 puzzles (4,500/4,500 total solves).
Report solver execution speed: median 1.02-1.85 ms per puzzle, with full 500-puzzle suites completing in 0.80-1.74 seconds total.
Report synthesis overhead: cost to generate code ranged from $0.003 (Haiku) to $0.063 (Opus), requiring 12-44 seconds to write (96-128 lines of code).
Report CRAM CPU re-implementation results across 3 random seeds: 496-497/500 puzzles solved in 2.51-2.52 seconds of training time.
Analyze inference speed: median latency 53.2-61.1 ms (p90 351-425 ms) with zero wrong stops (all failures due to move budget exhaustion at ~6.3 s).
Compare with the hand-set one-weight Hopfield energy: 497/500 solved (median 42.8 ms, p90 311 ms) with zero training time.
Evaluate constraint recovery: demonstrate 1.000 precision peer recovery (top-20 learned same-digit couplings correspond exactly to true Sudoku peers).
Highlight performance on direct LLM failure instances: learned CRAM solved 10/10 LLM test puzzles (0.3 ms to 1.29 s), including the two that defeated Opus and Sonnet in 66 ms and 122 ms.
Synthesize the core message: direct internal reasoning by frontier LLMs is an inefficient and unreliable tool for combinatorial puzzles.
Emphasize that programmatic synthesis via LLMs provides the optimal trade-off: pennies to synthesize, microseconds to execute, and perfect reliability.

Reiterate that CRAM can be replicated on a simple CPU in 2.5 seconds, but its parity with a hand-set Hopfield model confirms that Sudoku-Extreme measures constraint satisfaction rather than high-level emergent reasoning.
Caution against equating success on structured grid constraint satisfaction with broad cognitive reasoning in neural architectures.
Recommend that future benchmark suites decouple algorithmic search problems suitable for deterministic code from multi-step natural reasoning tasks.
Specify dataset splits and seed parameters used to extract 500 test puzzles from sapientinc/sudoku-extreme and 1,000 training boards.
Provide pseudocode and algorithmic parameters for pseudolikelihood estimation in NumPy and focused Gibbs sampling in C.
Document exact LLM prompt formulations and API configurations (adaptive thinking, effort high, max 32k tokens).
